title: Enable complete, patterned regeneration of complex mammalian structures

concept.text: The innovation would enable an adult mammal to rebuild an amputated complex structure with the right anatomy, integrated function and stable growth. A complete limb is the central example: regeneration would have to produce correctly positioned skeletal elements, muscles, nerves, blood vessels and skin, connected to the remaining body. Producing additional tissue alone would not establish this capability. This description defines the intended outcome; it is not an achieved result.

A central biological challenge is patterning competence: whether cells can respond to signals that organize regenerating tissue into the appropriate structure. The supplied axolotl study connects this competence to neural input, growth-factor signaling and changes in chromatin, the material that packages DNA and helps regulate gene activity. It provides a basis for investigating how regenerative cells acquire organizational capabilities, without establishing that the same intervention would enable mammalian regeneration.

significance.text: Regrowing a functional adult mammalian limb would demonstrate that a mammal can coordinate the reconstruction of multiple tissue types into a complex working structure after amputation. Its significance would lie in rebuilding anatomy in place while restoring its organization and function. The axolotl work helps explain why this is a distinct challenge: cells must become competent to interpret patterning signals that organize the growing tissue.

Conditional implications: if the capability could subsequently be made safe and effective in humans, it could create a way to restore structures lost through amputation. Discoveries might also inform regeneration of other tissues or organs. Neither outcome follows automatically from success in one mammalian species or one anatomical target; human treatment and other-organ regeneration would each require separate demonstrations.

The salamander comparison supplies a biological example and mechanistic questions, rather than a ready-made treatment strategy. The supplied paper identifies differences in cells' competence to respond to regenerative signals. A shared signaling component or chromatin response therefore cannot be assumed to constitute a universal master pathway that reconstructs limbs in mammals or humans.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is controlled, patterned reconstruction of an adult mammalian complex structure. The supplied paper describes mammalian limb regeneration as limited relative to axolotl regeneration and characterizes human regenerative potential in this context as restricted to the most distal digit region. Its discussion points to cellular competence as a barrier: regenerative signals must act on cells able to respond appropriately, including changes in cell state, proliferation, differentiation and interpretation of positional cues.

A mechanistic barrier is determining which neural, signaling and chromatin changes actually cause patterning competence, and which accompany it. The reviewed axolotl results connect nerve-dependent competence with FGF/BMP signaling and changes involving H3K27me3, a chemical modification of a histone protein associated with regulation of gene activity. These findings identify mechanisms to investigate; they do not establish that manipulating every associated chromatin change would induce competence, or that the mechanisms transfer to adult mammalian cells.

Engineering synthesis: a functional regenerated limb would also require coordinated growth, appropriate tissue proportions, functional nerve connections, a blood supply, attachment to the remaining limb and tissue maturation. Growth would need to stop at the appropriate size and leave stable tissue. These are requirements inferred from the intended functional outcome. The supplied source does not comprehensively establish the vascular coordination problem or demonstrate solutions to this full set of requirements.

current_state.text: Raymond et al. published “Neural regulation of H3K27me3 during the induction of patterning competency in regenerating Axolotl limb cells” on April 24, 2025, DOI 10.1038/s42003-025-08084-x. The supplied review verified the article's identity and examined its full main text, including methods and references. The experimental animals were axolotl salamanders. This is a published mechanistic study of salamander regeneration, not a demonstration of adult mammalian whole-limb regeneration.

The reviewed results describe nerve-dependent acquisition of patterning competence, experiments involving growth factors and inhibitors that address FGF/BMP signaling, and changes in H3K27me3 enrichment at patterning genes as limb cells transition toward competence. Together, these findings concern how regenerative cells become able to participate in organized limb formation. The chromatin observations should not be interpreted as proof that every identified mark causes competence; the reviewed discussion retains uncertainty about causal roles.

The evidence available through the supplied review has specific boundaries. Figure images, raw datasets and linked supplementary materials were not inspected, although the main-text extraction was reported as complete and untruncated. The bounded account above rests on that reviewed text and does not imply independent examination of the uninspected materials.

Evidence-scope limitation: no bounded freshness-search entries were supplied, so these inputs do not establish the latest field-wide position or whether the capability remained unachieved as of November 1, 2026. They establish a relevant 2025 axolotl result and provide no adult mammalian whole-limb demonstration. The absence of a newer demonstration from this record is not evidence that no such result exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently reproduce regeneration of a complete amputated limb in an adult mammal, with a prespecified amputation level and anatomical target. A prespecified complex limb segment beyond the naturally regenerative digit tip could establish a meaningful intermediate capability. A segment-level result would establish regeneration of that segment; whole-limb completion would require a complete limb. A small extension of digit-tip regeneration should not satisfy the whole-limb goal.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduced complete limb regeneration in an adult mammal

completion_criteria.text: Proposed anatomical and functional criteria: demonstrate correctly positioned skeletal elements, muscles, nerves, blood supply and skin integrated with the remaining limb. Prespecify benchmarks that assess tissue organization, useful movement and sensation, rather than relying on tissue volume or appearance alone. Measurements should make clear which functions are restored and how performance compares with appropriate controls.
completion_criteria.label: Correctly patterned, integrated limbs restore benchmarked movement and sensation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability and reproducibility criteria: use follow-up sufficient to assess controlled growth, tissue maturation, durable useful function and long-term stability. Independent groups should reproduce the result under clearly described conditions. These are proposed evaluation principles, not published consensus thresholds; the supplied material provides no justified numerical duration, success rate or functional cutoff.
completion_criteria.label: Durable useful function and controlled growth are independently reproduced

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: report the demonstrated species, adult ages, injury conditions, anatomical levels, treatment requirements, success rates and adverse outcomes. Replication across a finite set of conditions would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality. Success in one adult mammalian model would not by itself establish human clinical readiness or regeneration of other organs.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated regeneration scope and practical limits are fully reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BIO-07, “Reversibly restore youthful function across an aged organism,” overlaps through cell-state regulation, tissue maintenance and functional restoration. BIO-06 specifically concerns rebuilding missing anatomy with correct spatial organization. Restoring youthful function does not by itself replace an amputated limb, and regenerating a limb would not establish rejuvenation across an organism.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-03, “Predict the effects of genome changes across biological contexts,” and BIO-04, “Create an experimentally predictive virtual cell,” could help investigate how cells respond to candidate regenerative interventions. Their endpoints are predictive capabilities; BIO-06 requires physical reconstruction and integrated function across multiple tissues in an animal. Success at predicting cellular behavior would not itself demonstrate the required anatomical organization.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-10, “Observe molecular state and dynamics inside living cells at scale,” and BIO-14, “Establish causal functions for noncoding elements and poorly understood proteins,” overlap with the measurement and causal interpretation of regenerative cell states. Such capabilities could help distinguish molecular changes that accompany competence from those that produce it. Observation and molecular annotation remain distinct from inducing complete regeneration.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-15, “Deliver programmable genome editors selectively to diverse cells in the body,” could provide an enabling route if regeneration eventually requires genetic interventions in particular cell populations. Selective delivery would address access to those cells; it would not determine which interventions generate correct positional information, coordinated growth or mature limb function. The supplied evidence does not establish genome editing as necessary for this concept.

Roster-based synthesis: BIO-09, “Observe and causally test whole-brain computation at cellular resolution,” and BIO-13, “Establish the physical mechanisms that store and retrieve a long-term memory,” share an interest in nervous-system function but have different endpoints. BIO-06 requires neural integration adequate for useful movement and sensation in regenerated anatomy. It does not require a complete account of whole-brain computation or long-term memory, and success in those concepts would not demonstrate limb reconstruction.

unresolved_issues: The supplied inputs do not establish the field's latest state or whether adult mammalian whole-limb regeneration remained unachieved as of November 1, 2026.
Which neural, FGF/BMP and H3K27me3 changes causally establish patterning competence, and which accompany it, remains incompletely resolved in the supplied account.
Whether the reviewed axolotl mechanisms can be transferred or adapted to adult mammalian cells remains undemonstrated here.
The intended experimental target, mammalian species, amputation level, functional benchmarks, acceptable success rate and sufficient follow-up duration remain to be specified.
Figure images, raw datasets and linked supplements were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting independent assessment beyond the reviewed main text.

The original broad scarring assertion and detailed vascular coordination claim lack direct substantiation in the supplied evidence; this record narrows or labels them as inference rather than treating them as disproven.

brief.title: Regrowing a complete, working limb
possible: An adult mammal could regrow an amputated limb with bones, muscles, nerves, blood vessels and skin arranged correctly and connected to the body. The rebuilt limb would restore movement and sensation, and stop growing at the right size.
why: For people who have lost a limb, a safe human treatment could offer a way to rebuild the missing structure in place. Achieving this would mean coordinating many tissues into a working whole.

sources.who: Michael J Raymond Jr., Catherine D McCusker and colleagues
sources.showed: In axolotl salamanders, FGF and BMP, proteins that signal cells, made wound cells able to respond to signals that organize limb tissue. Nerves helped cells acquire this ability.
sources.quote: a combination of FGF and BMP signaling is sufficient to induce patterning competency in limb wound cells
sources.cited_for: Cells must acquire the ability to respond to signals that organize a regenerating limb.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish that the same treatment gives adult mammalian cells this ability.

sources.who: Ling Yu, Ken Muneoka and colleagues
sources.showed: This preprint reports that sequential treatment with growth-signaling proteins regenerated missing digit bones and a joint complex in newborn mice.
sources.quote: Coordination of the blastema-dependent and blastema-independent responses result in the complete regeneration of all amputated skeletal structures.
sources.cited_for: Newborn mouse wounds can rebuild missing skeletal structures beyond the naturally regenerating digit tip.
sources.not_established: Regrowing digit bones in newborn mice does not establish complete limb regeneration or restored movement and sensation in adults.

sources.who: Ling Yu, Ken Muneoka and colleagues at Tulane University
sources.showed: BMP2, a growth-signaling protein, stimulated bone regrowth after digit amputations in newborn mice and hindlimb amputations in adults. Growth stayed within the amputated bone segment.
sources.quote: Thus, the BMP2-induced regenerative response is restricted to the individual skeletal element that is amputated.
sources.cited_for: Adult mammalian amputation wounds can respond with organized bone regrowth.
sources.not_established: The response did not rebuild joints, more distant bones or a complete working limb.

sources.who: Ling Yu, Lindsay A Dawson, Ken Muneoka and colleagues
sources.showed: Growth-signaling proteins induced bone and joint regeneration in mouse digits. Adult mice also formed joint-like structures, although responses varied.
sources.quote: Combining BMP2 and BMP9 treatments in sequence stimulates the regeneration of bone and joint.
sources.cited_for: Induced regeneration can rebuild joint structures as well as bone.
sources.not_established: Joint structures alone do not establish useful movement, sensation or complete limb reconstruction.

sources.who: Justin A Varholick, Malcolm Maden and colleagues, University of Florida
sources.showed: Spiny mice rebuilt several tissues after ear wounds, but replacement was uneven and incomplete. Older animals healed more slowly.
sources.quote: All regenerated tissue had less cartilage and muscle than uninjured tissue, declining proximal to distal.
sources.cited_for: Closing a wound can leave substantial gaps in the tissues being replaced.
sources.not_established: Ear wound closure does not establish complete anatomical restoration or regeneration of an amputated limb.

shown: Mouse studies have induced parts of the rebuilding process: bone regrowth in adult hindlimbs, joint-like structures in adult digits, and replacement of missing digit bones and joints in newborns.
Raymond and colleagues showed how axolotl wound cells acquire the ability to follow signals that organize limb tissue. That provides a mechanism to investigate in mammals.
missing: Independent groups would need to reproduce complete limb regrowth in an adult mammal.
The rebuilt tissues would need to connect with the body and restore measured movement and sensation.
Growth would need to stop appropriately, with useful function and stable tissue lasting over time.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce complete adult mammalian limb regrowth
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce complete limb regrowth from a predefined amputation level in an adult mammal. Rebuilding a smaller segment would establish an intermediate result.

milestones.label: Correct anatomy restores measured movement and sensation
milestones.explanation: The limb would have to contain correctly arranged, connected tissues and meet predefined movement and sensation benchmarks. This would establish that the rebuilt anatomy works.

milestones.label: Useful function lasts and growth stays controlled across teams
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce tissue maturation, controlled growth and lasting useful function over sufficient follow-up. This would establish durable reconstruction.

milestones.label: The demonstrated scope and practical limits are fully reported
milestones.explanation: Results would have to describe species, adult ages, injuries, amputation levels, treatments, success rates and adverse outcomes. This would define where regeneration works and its practical limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear which nerve signals and changes in DNA packaging cause cells to respond to organizing signals, rather than accompany that ability.
Whether axolotl mechanisms can be adapted to adult mammalian cells remains unresolved.
The appropriate functional benchmarks, success rate and follow-up duration still need to be defined.

page.title: Adult mammalian limb regeneration
page.definition: An adult mammal regrows the anatomical structures lost through limb amputation, restoring movement and sensation. The completion benchmark is a whole-limb demonstration in adult wild-type mice.

goal.need: GAO reported on 23 October 2024 that more than 2 million people in the United States live with loss of all or part of an arm or leg. NICHD’s limb-regeneration programme targets whole-limb regeneration or lengthening of short residual stumps after injury or amputation.

statements.body: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD)
statements.quote: Advance the ability to regenerate human limbs by using emerging technologies to activate the body’s own growth pathways and processes.
statements.context: An aspirational strategic-plan goal quoted in NICHD’s request for information on limb regeneration.

statements.body: European Research Council-funded SigReg project, coordinated by the Max Planck Society
statements.quote: whether grafting signaling center cells can induce regeneration programs following mouse digit amputations.
statements.context: The third objective in the project’s published grant record; the project uses adult mouse amputation models.

completion.title: Regenerated adult mouse limbs pass motor, sensory and blinded observational tests reproducibly.
completion.criterion: In experiments with ethics approval, adult wild-type mice reproducibly regrow amputated limbs. Their performance on a standard motor-function battery must be indistinguishable from controls; sensation in the regrown limb must also be indistinguishable. Blinded observers must be unable to identify which limb regenerated using noninvasive observational data.
completion.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, The Millennium Problems for Biology, problem 06, “Somatic limb regeneration”; published challenge specification.
completion.threshold_quote: must perform indistinguishably from controls in a standard battery of motor function tests
completion.basis: This external challenge specifies an adult mammalian model and requires reproducible limb regrowth, motor recovery, sensory recovery and observational indistinguishability. Its initial specification was published on 19 September 2026. It is a developer-proposed benchmark; its statistical margins and follow-up requirements remain unspecified.

milestones.title: An adult mammalian amputation regenerates patterned bone continuous with the severed skeletal element.
milestones.criterion: Induce stump-continuous, distally patterned bone regeneration within the severed skeletal element. Yu et al. (2012) applied BMP2, a bone-growth signal, two weeks after mid-shank amputation in 8–10-week-old mice. Three treated limbs elongated by a mean 3.04 mm (SD 0.07 mm), versus 1.31 mm (SD 0.33 mm) in controls; 1/3 restored distal tibia–fibula fusion. Follow-up was 8–10 weeks after amputation. These measurements are reported results, not success cutoffs.
milestones.set_by: Regeneration researchers’ anatomical convention of segment-specific skeletal regeneration, applied by Yu et al. in adult mouse hindlimbs.
milestones.threshold_quote: Thus, the BMP2-induced regenerative response is restricted to the individual skeletal element that is amputated.

milestones.title: A mammalian digit regenerates a joint cavity and cartilage on both adjoining bone surfaces.
milestones.criterion: A regenerated digit joint has a central cavity and articular cartilage on both adjoining bone surfaces. On 5 February 2019, Yu et al. reported joint regeneration in 56/80 neonatal digits after BMP2 followed seven days later by BMP9; histology identified the complete joint arrangement. Adult BMP9-treated digits formed a cavity in 1/5 specimens at 14 days after treatment, without demonstrating that complete cartilage arrangement.
milestones.set_by: Anatomical convention for a complete synovial joint, explicitly defined and applied by Yu et al.; the complete-joint experiment used neonatal mouse digits.
milestones.threshold_quote: The digit synovial joint is a tri-layered structure consisting of a central cavity with two articular cartilage layers associated with the adjoining bone elements.

milestones.title: A mammalian digit replaces every skeletal structure removed by a middle-phalanx amputation.
milestones.criterion: Replace the amputated middle-phalanx segment, terminal phalanx, sesamoid bone embedded in a tendon, and joint complex. The peer-reviewed report of 17 April 2026 used mice amputated at three days old. At 45 days after sequential FGF2 and BMP2 treatment, 44/44 digits formed ectopic bone and 21/44 formed two elements. Histology identified imperfect terminal-phalanx-like and sesamoid-like structures with connective-tissue attachments. These findings support skeletal reconstruction without establishing normal adult digits or whole limbs.
milestones.set_by: Regeneration researchers’ convention that regeneration replaces the structures removed at the amputation level; skeletal completeness was assessed by Yu et al. in neonatal mouse digits.
milestones.threshold_quote: Together the blastema-dependent and blastema-independent responses can result in the regeneration of all skeletal structures removed by amputation.

milestones.title: Blinded observers cannot identify which adult mouse limb was regenerated.
milestones.criterion: After limb amputation in an adult wild-type mouse, blinded observers cannot identify the regenerated limb using noninvasive observational data. This is the observational component of the published whole-limb challenge; motor performance, sensation and reproducibility are additional completion requirements.
milestones.set_by: FutureHouse and Edison Scientific, observational endpoint within problem 06 of The Millennium Problems for Biology; specified for adult wild-type mice.
milestones.threshold_quote: must not be capable of distinguishing which limb was regrown

not_found: No published adult wild-type mouse whole-limb result meeting the challenge was located through 14 November 2026.
No specification of the challenge’s amputation level, motor-test battery, equivalence margins, minimum sample size, success fraction or follow-up duration was located.
The adult hindlimb control-group sample size was not located in Yu et al. (2012).

results.finding: Sequentially treated neonatal mouse digits showed a joint regeneration response in 37/44 specimens.
results.detail: The study describes a regenerated synovial cavity and associated skeletal tissue, but does not demonstrate articular cartilage on both adjoining bone surfaces.
results.quote:
In addition, the distal-ventral skeletal 
response correlates positionally with the early joint regeneration response although  the FGF2 response 
frequency (30.3%) was greatly enhanced after BMP2 treatment (84.1%, 37/44) .

results.finding: After sequential treatment, 23/44 amputated neonatal mouse digits formed two ectopic bones.
results.detail: Histology identified P3-like and sesamoid-like elements with connective-tissue attachments. The text does not establish replacement of the amputated P2 segment together with all distal structures in the same digit.
results.quote:
Based on terminal µCT imaging (45 DPT), all digits displayed a skeletal response w ith the majority of digits 
forming one (40.9%, 18/44; Fig 3B) or two (52.3%, 23/44; Fig 3C) ect opic bones, and 2 digits (4.5%) formed 3 
ectopic bones (Supplemental Figure 7).

results.finding: BMP2-treated adult mouse limbs: 1 of 3 showed distal tibia–fibula fusion after amputation.
results.detail: All three treated limbs showed distal elongation. The fusion in one limb supported distal patterning; the response remained confined to the amputated skeletal elements.
results.quote: In the BMP2 group, one sample (n = 1/3; 33%) showed skeletal elongation and complete fusion of the tibia and fibula distal to the amputation, whereas the other two samples showed distal elongation of the tibia and fibula without distal fusion.

results.finding: BMP2-treated neonatal digits showed no evidence of P2/P3 joint regeneration; sample size was not specified for this observation.
results.detail: The study did not identify a joint cavity or articular cartilage on both adjoining bone surfaces.
results.quote: Analysis of whole-mount Alizarin red stained samples indicate that the induced regenerative response is restricted to the distal region of the P2 element; we found no evidence for the regeneration of the P2/P3 joint or the P3 element.

results.finding: BMP2-treated neonatal digits restored P2 length to 88% of unamputated controls; the quantitative groups contained 24–36 digits each.
results.detail: The induced response replaced part of the amputated P2 element, but the authors found no evidence of P2/P3 joint or P3 regeneration.

results.finding: Sequential BMP2/BMP9 treatment regenerated joints in 56 of 80 neonatal mouse digits.
results.detail: Histology identified a central cavity and articular cartilage on both adjoining surfaces. BMP9 followed BMP2 by seven days.

results.finding: In adult mice, 4 of 5 BMP2-treated amputated digits formed a distal bone callus continuous with the P2 stump.
results.detail: Regenerated P2 bone restored pre-amputation length and showed distal curvature and tendon attachment sites, supporting patterned regeneration. Articular cartilage, the joint and the P3 element were not restored.
